what_it_does: Solid-state drives (SSDs) can compress data before storing it, shrinking files and reclaiming storage space. A new type of SSD interface called ZNS (Zoned Namespace) imposes a strict rule: data must be written sequentially into each zone, like filling a notebook from front to back. This rule makes it impossible to use traditional in-drive compression transparently, because compression produces variable-length chunks — you would not know where a compressed chunk ends and the next begins when reading back, and you cannot easily reclaim the freed space without being able to rewrite already-written zones. CCZNS (Collaborative Compression for ZNS) breaks the deadlock by splitting responsibilities: the SSD's hardware still does the fast compression math, but instead of hiding the results, it tells the host computer exactly where each compressed chunk lands and how big it is. The host software (in this case, a storage engine called ZenFS used with the RocksDB database) uses those measurements to manage address bookkeeping and reclaim freed space. This collaboration lets both sides do what they are good at — the SSD compresses fast, the host manages the address space flexibly.
